Pathologic diagnosis is required and tissue is obtained by endoscopic biopsy and cytology. C
Tumor location and staging determine therapeutic options. B
Locoregional disease is treated with curative intent with multimodality therapy (radiation, chemotherapy, with or without surgery). A
Many patients present with metastatic disease, where the goal of therapy is to provide palliation of symptoms. C

background.definition: A malignancy of the esophagus, usually an adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma but occasionally a small cell carcinoma.

list.listitem: There are an estimated 15,500 new cases per year in the United States (4.6 per 10,00,000 persons per year).
The incidence of adenocarcinoma is on the rise. This histology now accounts for one-half of diagnoses compared with less than 10% in the 1960s.
Male incidence predominates (male to female ratio of 4:1); the median age at diagnosis is 69 years, with one-third under the age of 65.
24,785 cases in the United States (approximately 1 in 10,000 adults).
Sixth leading cause of cancer death among men in the United States.
Tobacco and alcohol abuse cause DNA mutations that lead to dysregulated cellular proliferation and malignant transformation in squamous cell carcinomas.

It has been proposed that gastroesophageal reflux causes Barrett's esophagus (metaplasia), which can progress to low- or high-grade dysplasia and ultimately to adenocarcinoma. However, Barrett's is common in patients without symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

A Scandinavian review following up endoscopies performed over a 32 year period with a cohort of 486,000 patients concluded that non-erosive gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) was not associated with increased risk of subsequent esophageal cancer as national cancer registry data enabled tracking of this population and showed similar incidence to background population. However erosive GERD did double risk of subsequent cancer although risk remained low overall.
The proportional increase in adenocarcinomas of the esophagus, compared with squamous cell carcinomas, is likely due to the increased incidence of obesity, reflux, and Barrett's esophagus.
Ninety percent of adenocarcinomas are found at the gastroesophageal junction, further implicating acid reflux as a potentially causative factor.
Esophageal cancer can spread through direct extension, through lymphatics, and less commonly through hematogenous dissemination.
Lymph node involvement is common in esophageal cancer, and primary esophageal tumors in the cervical, thoracic, or distal/gastroesophageal junction typically involve different lymph node groups.
Approximately 40% of patients have metastasis at initial presentation. Common sites of distant metastasis involve the lung, liver, bone, and adrenal glands.
PDL1 expression is associated with reduced overall survival in a recent meta-analysis but further investigation is required in relation to treatment options.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of prior squamous cell carcinoma

list.listitem: Screening for esophageal cancer is controversial. The Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines network only recommends upper endoscopy for patients with weight loss or with GERD and alarm symptoms. C
Surveillance at intervals based on length of involvement and presence of absence of dysplasia is recommended with Barrett's esophagus.B
A trial found that high dose PPI with aspirin resulted in lower mortality and progression in patients with Barrett's esophagus. B.

American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) guidelines (2025) recommend surveillance for patients with Barrett's Esophagus (BE) as follows:
Non-dysplastic BE < 1 cm: do not perform surveillance Non-dysplastic BE >= 1 cm: perform surveillance every 3 years, extend to 5 years in patients at lower risk of progression BE with low grade dysplasia: surveillance every 6 months for 1 year and then annually, OR endoscopic eradication therapy (EET). BE indefinite for dysplasia: annual endoscopic surveillance High grade dysplasia: definitive treatment.

A randomised controlled trial of 3453 patients with Barrett's esophagus (the BOSS trial) with median follow up over 12 years found no survival benefit for routine endoscopy every 2 years over endoscopy as needed based on symptoms only. There was no difference in cancer-specific survival (108 vs 106 deaths), time to diagnosis of cancer, or stage at diagnosis.
A large Chinese cluster randomized trial found that screening high risk areas in China was effective at reducing upper GI cancer mortality, but not in low risk areas.

The introduction of cytosponge sampling can be performed in primary care enabling less invasive diagnosis of Barrett's esophagus and possible early detection of esophageal cancer, but the overall population utility of this procedure awaits further evaluation.

A recent analysis with 910 patients undergoing capsule sponge combined with biomarker assessment demonstrated efficacy in stratifying into high and low risk groups. If more widely validated this would have practical benefit by avoiding endoscopic surveillance in the low risk group.
See chapters on GERD and Barrett's esophagus for a more detailed discussion.

A trial recruited 2557 patients randomising between high and low dose PPI plus or minus aspirin. This trial demonstrated that high dose PPI with aspirin did result in lower mortality and progression in patients with Barrett's esophagus.
Epidemiologic evidence suggests a protective effect for diets with adequate folate or rich in fruits and vegetables.
Suspect esophageal cancer in patients with dysphagia, cough, or hoarseness accompanied by weight loss, especially in a patient with a history of tobacco and/or alcohol use. C
Diagnosis requires pathologic evaluation of tissue to determine the presence of a malignancy. C
Stage is determined by imaging with endoscopic ultrasound, CT, and PET. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Long-standing symptoms of heartburn or history of exposure

list.listitem: Ninety percent of patients present with dysphagia and weight loss. Both typically present as progressive symptoms over weeks to months and may result in odynophagia. Patients may have a chronic cough, which could be due to tracheo-esophageal fistula.
Hoarseness suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
Lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, abdominal mass, or bone pain suggest the presence of distant metastasis.

A study of patients presenting with dysphagia identified six factors that predict the likelihood of esophageal cancer. It was increased in patients with weight loss greater than 3 kg, male sex, dysphagia not in the neck, no reflux, symptoms present more than 6 months, and age over 40 years.

Order esophageal endoscopy with biopsy to establish the diagnosis, to measure and localize the lesion, and to search for skip metastasis. Endoscopy combined with biopsy and cytology has a diagnostic accuracy of 99%.
Up to 40% of patients present with metastatic disease; therefore, the goal is to identify patients that have only localized disease for potentially curative treatment with multimodality therapies.
Recommended blood tests include CBC (to detect occult bleeding) and comprehensive panel. (Elevated AST/ALT or alkaline phosphatase is concerning for metastasis.)

Use CT and PET scan (or PET/CT) imaging to evaluate for the presence of metastatic disease. PET is more sensitive than CT, and detects metastasis in ~15% of patients who are negative by other imaging modalities.
If there is no evidence of metastatic disease, then the primary tumor is staged according to the American Joint Commission for Cancer criteria.
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration is preferred for evaluation of nodal staging.

Order direct laryngoscopy for patients with lesions of the cervical esophagus to evaluate for metachronous lesions. Order bronchoscopy for patients with tumors above or at the level of the carina to evaluate for tracheoesophagela fistula.
Surgical staging of patients is controversial, but abdominal laparoscopy and thoracoscopy can be considered.
A validated clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of esophageal cancer among patients presenting with dysphagia.

Risk factors for poor prognossis include age, sex, tumor stage, histology, resection margin status. education level, neoadjuvant therapy, reoperation within one month of primary surgery, and comorbidity based on the Charlson comorbidity index. A risk score was developed that had good calibration and area under the ROC curve of 0.76 in the validation group.

Another risk score for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma was developed and externally validated in two European populations; it includes age, sex, smoking, alcohol and BMI. The AUC for 5 year risk of cancer is 0.70 in the validation cohort. It is available at an online calculator.
Suspect esophageal cancer in patients with dysphagia, cough, or hoarseness accompanied by weight loss, especially in a patient with a history of tobacco and/or alcohol use.
Order a biopsy for patients with abnormal findings on upper endoscopy.
Diagnosis is established by pathologic evaluation of tissue. Endoscope-directed biopsy and brush cytology have a sensitivity that approaches 100%.

Curative treatment for esophageal cancer typically consists of combined therapy with radiation therapy and chemotherapy, with or without surgery. Some patients with small noncervical tumors may be candidates for surgery alone. A

Historically open surgery esophagectomy has carried risks of intra- and post-operative complications. The incidence of complications is lower with hybrid minimally invasive esophagectomy, without worsening of progression free survival. B
Surgical resection is a complex operation with high risk perioperative morbidity. High volume centres have improved outcomes with regards to 1 and 5 year survival. B

Nivolumab immunotherapy as adjuvant treatment following neo-adjuvant chemoradiation followed by complete surgical resection has demonstrated significant benefit in disease free survival (22.4 months vs. 11 months). B

Comparison of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy to neoadjuvant chemotherapy demonstrated improved 2-year survival and disease free survival for the group receiving immunotherapy for squamous cancers of the esophagus.
Many patients present with distant metastasis and undergo palliative therapy. C
Consider surgical resection as primary therapy for patients with stage I (T1N0M0) lesions of the thoracic esophagus and gastroesophageal junction.

Treat patients who have squamous esophageal cancers with concurrent chemotherapy and radiation; reserve surgery for salvage therapy. A Cochrane Systematic review used patient level data for 1147 patients from 5 RCTs who had been randomized to pre-operative radiation therapy or none and followed for up to 9 years. There was a trend toward lower mortality (3% at 2 years and 4% at 5 years, p = 0.06) in those receiving pre-operative radiation but the benefit is felt to be modest, at best.

Surgical resection is a complex operation with high risk perioperative morbidity. Review of patients receiving surgical resection as recorded on the national cancer database highlights that those who travelled to receive surgery at high volume centres had improved outcomes on one and five year survival.
High intensity interval training was shown in a small RCT to improve fitness pre-operatively in a deconditioned cohort with esophaeal or lung cancer.

A Cochrane review examined the role of pre-operative chemotherapy across 13 RCTs with a total of 2362 patients. The use of pre-operative chemotherapy achieved significant improvment in overall survival and increased the rate of R0 complete resection.

A trial randomized 438 patients with resectable locally advanced esophageal adenocarcinoma to perioperative chemotherapy with FLOT (fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel) plus surgery or preoperative chemoradiotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel plus surgery. At 3 years, overall survival was higher in the FLOT group (57.4% vs 50.4%, p = 0.01, NNT = 14).

A 2017 meta-analysis of 33 RCTs with over 6,000 patients suggests that neo-adjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery is the most effective treatment strategy in patients with resectable esophageal cancer.

A systematic review of 10 trials with 6462 patients demonstrated overall survival benefit sustained to 5 years follow-up with the addition of adjuvant systemic therapy following neoadjuvant therapy and surgery.

An individual patient data meta-analysis of 7 randomized or propensity score matched studies compared radiochemotherapy followed by active surveillance with standard esophagectomy in 453 patients with a clinically complete response following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Overall survival was similar but 40% of patients eventually underwent esophagectomy during the 5 year follow-up period, emphasizing the importance of rigorous adherence to the follow-up protocol.

In contrast a study with 274 patients who achieved clinical complete response following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy were randomised between surgery and continued surveillance. The 2-year survival was equivalent but with improved quality of life in the group not receiving surgery.

A large double-blind RCT (Checkmate 577) assessing the use of nivolumab immunotherapy as adjuvant treatment following neo-adjuvant chemoradiation followed by complete surgical resection has demonstrated significant benefit in disease free survival with the treated group achieving median DFS 22.4 months compared to 11 months in the placebo group.

For both advanced squamous carcinoma of the esophagus (Checkmate 648) and for locally advanced cancer esophageal junction/adenocarcinoma (Checkmate 649) the addition of nivolumab to chemotherapy significantly improved survival.

There is emerging evidence that neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy using immunotherapy upfront can improve overall and disease free survival in locally advanced squamous cancer of the esophagus. In an audit of database registered treatments the benefit of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy was postulated to be due to reduction in distant metastases.
Similarly overall and progression free survival benefit has been demonstrated with the addition of pembrolizumab immunotherapy to chemotherapy (Keynote 590 trial).
Treat all other patients without metastatic disease with combined radiation and chemotherapy, followed by surgical resection if appropriate.
Consider patients treated with surgery alone and found to have more extensive disease for postoperative chemotherapy and radiation.

Treat patients who have distant metastasis with palliative chemotherapy and best supportive care. Palliation of symptoms includes: stenting and/or radiation therapy for obstruction; radiation therapy or endoscopic therapy for bleeding from tumor site; narcotic analgesics or radiation therapy for pain; and G-tube placement or esophageal dilatation for nutrition.
Vitamin D does not increase survival in adults with digestive tract cancer including esophageal cancer.
A well designed Danish study found that patients with Barrett's esophagus progress to esophageal cancer at a rate of 0.12% per year.B

High-grade dysplasia progresses to cancer in 30% to 40% of cases, while low-grade dysplasia progresses much less commonly. Patients with longer duration of BE and older patients are at greater risk of progression to malignancy. B
Estimated 5-year survival for esophageal cancer: localized 30%, regional 15%, metastatic less than 5%. B

Patients with esophageal cancer are typically in their 60s and may have significant comorbidities. Results from clinical trials typically represent patients who are able to undergo therapy (good performance status, minimal weight loss, few comorbidities). B

Based on a Swedish population registry with 1542 patients surviving at least 90 days after surgery, predictors of 5 year all-cause mortality include increasing age, male sex, increasing pathological stage, non-radical resection, squamous cell carcinoma, and reoperation within 30 days.
A meta-analysis of over 12,000 samples indicates that loss and mutation of p53 and increased levels Ki67 predict malignant progression in Barrett's esophagus.
